analysis.one_liner: Replaces the ethanol-heavy renewable fuel mandate with a low-carbon fuel standard for transportation fuel.
analysis.headline: Senator Wyden's low-carbon fuel standard bill drew no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and never received a vote before the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This 2009 bill by Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) would have rewritten the federal rule that requires fuel refiners and blenders to mix renewable fuel into gasoline and diesel. Instead of counting any renewable fuel (like corn ethanol) toward a quota, refiners would have had to meet a "low-carbon" standard: starting in 2015, 10% of transportation fuel sold in the U.S. would have to be low-carbon, with that share rising by 1.5 percentage points each year until 2030, after which the EPA would set the levels based on specified criteria (CRS summary; bill text). Fuel that isn't low-carbon — principally conventional gasoline and diesel, and higher-carbon biofuels — would have to be offset by low-carbon alternatives. The bill included safeguards meant to prevent fuel suppliers from price-setting or other anticompetitive behavior (CRS summary). It was introduced on May 20, 2009, referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, and never advanced: it had zero cosponsors, no committee action, and no floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2011 (action history; cosponsors page).
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main gains would have been long-term: lower carbon emissions from transportation fuel and, per the bill's stated purposes, improved air quality (bill text). Producers of genuinely low-carbon fuels — advanced biofuels, natural gas, and electricity for vehicles — would have gained a guaranteed, growing market (CRS summary). Ordinary consumers would have gained indirectly through reduced climate and air-pollution harm, though the timing and size of those gains are diffuse.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-carbon fuel makers; the public's air and climate.

how_it_helps.text: Beginning January 1, 2015, the bill would have replaced the existing renewable fuel program with a low-carbon transportation fuel program, requiring 10% of transportation fuel sold or introduced into U.S. commerce to be low-carbon.
The low-carbon share would have increased by 1.5 percentage points each year until 2030, after which the EPA Administrator would set percentages for 2031 and beyond using specified criteria.

The bill would have amended the Clean Air Act to convert the renewable fuel standard into a low-carbon fuel standard, meaning compliance would be measured by carbon content rather than simply by whether a fuel is renewable.
The bill included provisions directing regulators to avoid price-setting and other anticompetitive behavior in the new fuel market.
Fuel suppliers could carry forward a low-carbon fuel deficit under conditions set out in the bill, giving them some flexibility in meeting the annual targets.

analysis.who_pays: The compliance costs would have fallen on petroleum refiners and fuel blenders, who would have had to purchase or produce low-carbon fuel to offset every gallon of conventional fuel they sold — and those costs would likely have been passed partly into fuel prices paid at the pump. The corn ethanol industry would also have lost the guaranteed demand it enjoys under the current renewable fuel standard, which this bill would have replaced, because corn ethanol has a higher carbon profile than the fuels the new standard favors.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil refiners, blenders, and pump prices; corn ethanol's mandate.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs on refiners and blenders would likely have been passed at least partly to consumers as higher gasoline and diesel prices, and opponents would have argued that the supply of genuinely low-carbon fuel was not yet large enough to meet the rising annual targets without price spikes.

Because the bill would have replaced the existing renewable fuel standard, it would have stripped corn ethanol of its guaranteed market share — a real cost that corn-state senators and the ethanol industry would have fought hard, and one reason the bill attracted zero cosponsors in a Senate where the current mandate is politically protected.

The annual percentage increases (1.5 points per year through 2030) were fixed in statute, giving regulators limited room to slow the ramp-up if low-carbon fuel supplies or infrastructure failed to develop on schedule.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside was broad but long-term: a fuel system that rewards carbon content rather than any renewable label, which would gradually cut transportation emissions and air pollution. The downside was more immediate and concentrated: refiners would face new compliance costs likely shared with drivers at the pump, and the ramp-up was fixed in law even if low-carbon fuel supply lagged. A well-designed standard of this kind can deliver net public benefit, but this bill never got far enough for the design to be tested, amended, or debated — its zero cosponsors meant the trade-offs were never weighed on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced, never received a single cosponsor, and died there when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) introduced the bill on May 20, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day.
No cosponsors ever joined the bill.
The Environment and Public Works Committee took no recorded action on the bill, and it never reached the Senate floor for a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the existing renewable fuel standard — with its guaranteed demand for ethanol — stayed in place. Petroleum refiners avoided a new low-carbon compliance obligation, and the corn ethanol industry kept its mandated market. Ordinary people got none of the bill's promised emissions and air-quality benefits, but also avoided the compliance costs that would have been partly passed to them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil refiners and the ethanol mandate's beneficiaries.

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.role: Sponsor (introduced the bill; its only supporter in the Senate)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered sponsor introductory remarks on May 20, 2009; no other senator cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held and no cosponsor joined, so the bill's support was one senator from each chamber's majority party's caucus — there was no party-line fight to measure; the committee simply never acted.

industries.note: Refiners and blenders would have had to ensure 10% of transportation fuel was low-carbon in 2015, rising 1.5 points a year to 2030, paying for low-carbon fuel to offset every conventional gallon — costs typically passed partly to drivers. The industry benefited from the bill's death.

The bill would have replaced the renewable fuel standard that guarantees corn ethanol a market share with a standard measured by carbon content, which disfavors corn ethanol. The industry's interest in preserving the current mandate runs against a stricter carbon-based standard but is not simply opposed to renewable fuel overall.

industries.industry: Advanced biofuels and low-carbon fuel producers (including natural gas and electricity for vehicles)
industries.note: A rising mandatory low-carbon share would have created a guaranteed and growing market for fuels with low carbon intensity, the same fuels that reduce emissions for the public.
